title: What video gear does your exec or in-house creator need?
answer: Most B2B teams need less gear than they think. Under $500 buys a 4K webcam, a decent USB mic, one light, a stand, foam panels and headphones, which is plenty for a founder recording at a desk. Spend $500 to $1,500 when someone records weekly, and $1,500+ when video is a core channel and the setup needs to look like a studio. Buy audio and light before camera.
author: Ademola Adelakun

body.text: What should you buy first when you equip someone for video?

Buy for sound first, light second and camera third. Viewers forgive a slightly soft image, but they click away from echoey, tinny audio in seconds, and bad lighting makes even a great camera look cheap. So if you're equipping your CEO, a product marketer or an in-house creator, put the money where the viewer notices it.

The good news is that none of this needs a production budget. Every kit below fits on a desk, sets up in an afternoon and runs off a laptop. The goal is a setup your exec can sit down at and record without calling anyone for help, because the easier it is to hit record, the more often it happens.

items.label: Audio
items.text: A dedicated mic plus a little acoustic treatment. This is the single biggest jump in perceived quality.

items.label: Light
items.text: One soft key light in front of the face, then a fill light once you upgrade. Window light is free but changes all day.

items.label: Camera
items.text: A good 4K webcam covers most needs. Move to a real camera when video is a weekly habit, not a quarterly one.

items.label: Mounting
items.text: Stands and arms keep the camera at eye level and the desk clear, which matters more than people expect.

body.text: Which kit should your team buy?

Match the kit to how often the person records and where the video goes. A founder recording a few LinkedIn clips a month needs the basic kit. Someone filming every week for sales and social should have the intermediate kit. If video is a core channel, or the setup doubles as a podcast studio, go advanced.

rows: An exec recording occasional talking-head clips and async updates
A weekly recorder: a founder-led series, sales videos, webinars
A dedicated in-house creator, podcast or studio-style setup

body.text: All prices below are approximate as of when we built this list, so check current pricing through the B&H link on each product before you buy.

The basic kit gets an exec from laptop-webcam footage to clean, clear video for under $500. Each category has a primary pick and a cheaper alternative, so choose one of each. The primary picks total about $464 and the budget picks about $290.

body.text: What's in the intermediate kit ($500 to $1,500)?

The intermediate kit is for someone who records every week. It adds a tracking webcam (or a real camera), a mic that can grow into XLR, and a two-light setup that removes shadows. Pick either the Insta360 webcam or the Sony ZV-1F, not both. The full list comes to about $1,519.

rows: 4K webcam with physical gimbal tracking. Frames you automatically even if you move around. Great if you stand or use a whiteboard.
Dedicated vlog camera with USB webcam mode. Massive quality jump over any webcam. Wide f/2.0 lens. Choose the webcam or the camera, not both.
Dual USB-C and XLR. Grow into XLR later without replacing the mic. Podcast-quality audio.
App-controlled, 2800 lumens, desk clamp mount. Set-and-forget studio lighting.
Second light to fill shadows. Pairs well with the Elgato Key Light as main.
Flexible legs wrap around anything. Great for desk, shelf or travel setups.
Covers ~52 sq ft. Triangular groove design breaks up sound waves effectively.
Industry standard. Same pick as the basic kit, no need to upgrade headphones at this tier.
Pull-up green screen, retracts into its case. Instant clean background. Optional, depends on the office setup.

body.text: The advanced kit turns an office into a small studio: an interchangeable-lens camera, a broadcast mic with an interface, two app-controlled lights and diffusers that look good on camera and treat the room. It's the right call for a dedicated in-house creator or a podcast. The full list comes to about $2,390.

rows: Interchangeable lens, 4K/60p, USB-C streaming. Best content creator camera under $1K.
For HDMI output at 4K. Use it when you want max quality over USB streaming. Optional, since the camera has USB-C streaming.
Built-in preamp, no Cloudlifter needed. The podcast and broadcast standard. Sounds incredible.

App-controlled panel, desk clamp. Consistent color temperature for video.
Portable, rechargeable, app-controlled. Perfect as a fill or hair light.
Desk clamp + articulating arm. The camera floats at the right height and saves desk space.

Extra-wide pull-up green screen for a standing desk or wider shots. Optional, depends on the office setup.
Low-profile boom arm. Keeps the mic off the desk and out of the frame.

body.text: How do you set the gear up so it looks good on camera?

Put the camera at eye level, the key light in front of and slightly to the side of the face, and the mic as close to the mouth as the frame allows. Those three choices do more for the final video than any upgrade in the tables above.

items.label: Camera height
items.text: Eye level or a touch above. A laptop camera looking up the nose undercuts every point your exec makes.

items.label: Light
items.text: Face the light source, never a bright window behind you. Set every light to the same color temperature.

items.label: Background
items.text: Clean and a little depth behind the speaker. A green screen only helps if someone will actually key it out in the edit.

items.label: Sound check
items.text: Record 10 seconds and play it back on headphones before every session. It catches hums, echo and the wrong mic input.

body.text: For the on-camera side, read [how to film yourself](/playbook/how-to-film-yourself). If the person in front of the gear is your CEO, [how to get your CEO on camera](/playbook/ceo-on-camera) covers the part no kit can fix.
When is gear not the problem?

Gear is rarely what holds a B2B video program back. Most teams that stall have a perfectly good camera and no plan for what to film, who it's for or how sales will use it. So buy the kit, then spend most of your energy on the strategy and the edit.

If your marketing team has quietly become the video department, [the voluntold video department](/playbook/in-house-video-production) walks through what it really takes to run video in-house, and the [in-house vs. agency editor breakdown](/blog/in-house-vs-agency-video-editor) helps you decide who should cut the footage your new kit produces.

closing.text: A good kit makes recording easy, and the next step is making sure your exec looks and sounds natural in front of it.
